newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn minister gets support from CDU pensions group.
newsitem.headline: Bonn minister gets support from CDU pensions group.

text.p: A committee of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday gave broad backing to a pension reform plan by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem which has sparked arguments in the CDU and the coalition.
Twenty out of 30 members of the CDU pensions committee backed Bluem's proposal with only minor adjustments after a two-day meeting in Windhagen near Bonn.
A leading member of the commission, Heiner Geissler, said he expected the party executive under Kohl, who has clashed with Bluem over the reform, to take the same line at a meeting on Wednesday.

Bluem's plan involves raising contributions while reducing payouts in response to the growing proportion of pensioners. It also calls for other welfare benefits which are paid out of the pensions fund to be paid for out of taxes instead.
The proposal, developed by a commission of experts chaired by Bluem, clashed with an ambitious tax cutting proposal put forward by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
Bluem's approach irritated Kohl and angered his Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners, who want a more aggressive reform and no tax increases.
But party sources close to the chancellor said he agreed with Bluem on the need to preserve the current pay-as-you-go pensions system, where those in work pay for those who have retired.
Kohl's anger was directed more at Bluem's failure to follow agreed procedures than at the substance of the plan, they said.
Bluem, Kohl's longest serving minister and widely seen as an important symbol of the CDU's social conscience, also attempted to smooth over the disagreement.
"I have no doubts about the chancellor's trustworthiness," he told the daily Bild, according to an advance release from Tuesday's edition.
"That wasn't and isn't my point and if that impression has arisen I regret it... We are old comrades and have fought many battles together."
The party's pensions commission agreed with Bluem's proposal to cut the level of pensions to 64 percent of average earnings by 2030 from 70 percent currently.

But while Bluem suggested that contributions should fall from just over 20 percent now to 18.7 percent in 2010, before starting to climb again towards 23 percent, the commission said they should not drop below 20 percent.
This would allow the creation of a "generation fund" to limit future increases in contributions.

The commission agreed with Bluem's proposal that non-pension items such as maternity and child benefits should be financed not from the pension fund but from a "family fund" paid for from tax revenues.
And it agreed with Bluem in rejecting Waigel's plan to increase tax on pensions.
It did not say, though, whether the shortfall in revenue should come from higher value added tax or a tax on fuel.
